summary: Describes operators added to the UCSB On-Line System so its users could reach the ARPANET. They are defined at level I of a system named NET and serve as an interface to the local Network Control Program. As in RFC 119 and RFC 120, each non-closed socket has a completion code variable.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 121 describes terminal operators that let UCSB On-Line System users access the network through the local NCP. Users can open sockets, send and receive data, inspect status, and interact with a remote system.

subtitle: Interactive operators for UCSB On-Line System users to access the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: UCSB On-Line System users needed terminal operators for using the network through the site's Network Control Program.
tldr.mechanism: Operators such as OPEN, CLOSE, SEND, RECEIVE, and CHECK perform socket operations and report their status to the user.
tldr.outcome: RFC 121 documents a site-specific terminal interface for network operations, including message formats for display and key input.

today: RFC 121 documents network operators for the UCSB On-Line System. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces it.

sections.title: Operators for Network Access
sections.content:
The operators are defined for Level I of the UCSB On-Line System's NET system. They provide an interface between terminal users and the local Network Control Program (NCP).

Each socket that is not closed has a completion-code variable. It identifies the socket and receives a code indicating the result of an operation. The RFC specifies that site number information for local sockets is implicit.
sections.plainLanguage: On-Line System users enter operators at the terminal instead of managing NCP messages directly. Completion codes report what happened to each socket operation.

sections.title: Opening, Listening, and Closing
sections.content:
OPEN provides three operations: CONNECT requests a connection to a foreign socket, LISTEN waits for a connection request to a local socket, and ACCEPT completes a connection after a LISTEN. CONNECT and LISTEN require the local socket to be closed.

CLOSE returns the local socket to the closed state. It refuses a pending connection request, aborts a pending connection attempt, or allows data in transit to reach the foreign socket before closing an established connection.
sections.plainLanguage: OPEN can place a call, wait for one, or accept one. CLOSE ends a connection after handling any request or data still in progress.

sections.title: Sending, Receiving, and Status
sections.content:
SEND transmits data through a local send socket, and RECEIVE gets data through a local receive socket. Processing at the terminal waits for the operation to complete. The operators also provide CHECK to display socket state and IDENTIFY to find the socket associated with a completion-code variable.

SIGNAL sends a user-defined signal to the foreign process. PURGE closes the sockets in use at the terminal and dissociates their completion-code variables.
sections.plainLanguage: SEND and RECEIVE transfer data over open sockets. CHECK displays their status, while SIGNAL and PURGE provide additional control.

sections.title: Messages for the On-Line System
sections.content:
Messages consist of an operation code, a length in bits, and text. The operation code is one byte and the length is two bytes. Code 0 is NOP, code 1 carries EBCDIC characters for display, code 2 carries key codes to execute as received, and code 3 delays key execution until all data for the receive operation arrives.

A NOP header serves as a trailer for a string of messages. The RFC says these are default conventions that appropriate programming may override.
sections.plainLanguage: The message header tells the On-Line System what the text contains. A NOP header marks the end of a sequence of messages.
